chief_complaint: rapid jaundice, dark tea urine, and severe fatigue
hpi_details: 38F presenting with acute hemolytic anemia, scleral icterus, splenomegaly, spherocytes on smear, and strongly positive Direct Antiglobulin Test (Coombs IgG).
ideas: She thinks she contracted viral hepatitis or acute liver failure from contaminated food she ate over the weekend.
concerns: She is worried that her liver is completely failing and that she will need an urgent organ transplant, leaving her unable to care for her young children.
expectations: She hopes for comprehensive liver blood tests and medication to clear up the jaundice so she can regain her strength.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (Warm AIHA) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (Warm AIHA) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes first-line high-dose corticosteroids to suppress autoantibody-mediated red cell destruction, with escalation to rituximab or splenectomy for steroid-refractory disease, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: rapid jaundice, dark tea urine, and severe fatigue
Key HPI features: 38F presenting with acute hemolytic anemia, scleral icterus, splenomegaly, spherocytes on smear, and strongly positive Direct Antiglobulin Test (Coombs IgG).

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 37.2C, HR 108, BP 110/70. Scleral icterus, mucosal pallor, mild splenomegaly (spleen tip palpable), no lymphadenopathy. Bloods: Hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, reticulocyte count 12% (elevated), LDH markedly elevated, haptoglobin undetectable, total bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL with indirect fraction 3.6 mg/dL. Peripheral smear shows spherocytes and polychromasia. Direct Antiglobulin Test (Coombs) strongly positive for IgG.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (Warm AIHA).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cold agglutinin disease (cold AIHA) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rapidly falling hemoglobin or symptoms of severe anemia (chest pain, breathlessness) — may need urgent transfusion.
management_principles: Assess hemodynamic stability; transfuse crossmatch-compatible (least incompatible) packed RBCs if symptomatic or hemoglobin critically low, recognizing the autoantibody may complicate crossmatching
Start high-dose corticosteroids (Prednisone 1mg/kg/day) as first-line therapy to suppress hemolysis
Supplement folic acid 1mg daily given ongoing hemolysis and increased red cell turnover
Escalate to Rituximab or splenectomy if steroid-refractory; screen for secondary causes (lupus, CLL, lymphoma, drug-induced hemolysis)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia Warm AIHA: rapid jaundice, dark tea urine, and severe fatigue. 38F presenting with acute hemolytic anemia, scleral icterus, splenomegaly, spherocytes on smear, and strongly positive Direct Antiglobulin Test (Coombs IgG).
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 37.2C, HR 108, BP 110/70. Scleral icterus, mucosal pallor, mild splenomegaly (spleen tip palpable), no lymphadenopathy. Bloods: Hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, reticulocyte count 12% (elevated), LDH markedly elevated, haptoglobin undetectable, total bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL with indirect fraction 3.6 mg/dL. Peripheral smear shows spherocytes and polychromasia. Direct Antiglobulin Test (Coombs) strongly positive for IgG.
reference_soap.assessment: Warm Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (Warm AIHA) presenting with acute IgG-mediated extravascular hemolysis, jaundice, and symptomatic anemia.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Assess hemodynamic stability; obtain a type and crossmatch, transfusing least-incompatible packed RBCs if symptomatic or hemoglobin critically low. 2. Start high-dose corticosteroids: Prednisone 1mg/kg/day as first-line therapy. 3. Supplement folic acid 1mg daily given ongoing hemolysis. 4. If steroid-refractory after 1-3 weeks, escalate to Rituximab; consider splenectomy for relapsed/refractory disease. 5. Screen for secondary causes (ANA/lupus workup, CLL/lymphoma evaluation, recent new medications) and refer to hematology for ongoing monitoring of Hgb, reticulocytes, and LDH.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia Warm AIHA
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for rapid jaundice, dark tea urine, and severe fatigue
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for hematology_oncology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: IgG autoantibodies coat red blood cells at body temperature, marking them for destruction by the spleen, causing rapid jaundice, dark urine, and fatigue with a positive direct Coombs test.
red_flags: Rapidly falling hemoglobin or symptoms of severe anemia (chest pain, breathlessness) — may need urgent transfusion

must_ask.say: How quickly did the yellowing of your eyes or skin come on?
Has your urine looked unusually dark, like tea?
How severe is your fatigue — is it affecting your ability to function?
Do you have any other autoimmune conditions, like lupus?
Are you taking any new medications recently?

history.answer: My eyes turned yellow a couple of days ago, and my urine has become very dark like black tea. I have also felt overwhelmingly exhausted.
It came on very quickly about three days ago. My whites of the eyes looked yellowish, and over the past forty-eight hours, the yellow color and exhaustion have gotten much worse.
Yes, it started turning dark brown, almost the color of black tea or cola, about two days ago. It stays dark every time I go to the bathroom.
No, my stools look normal brown. They are definitely not pale, white, or clay-colored.
No, my skin has not been itchy at all, and I have not had any hives or rashes.
No, I do not have any stomach pain, cramps, or pain under my right ribs, even after eating greasy food.
I felt a little warm yesterday, but I have not had shaking chills or high fevers.
The exhaustion is debilitating. Even walking from the bedroom to the kitchen leaves me drained and needing to sit down.
Whenever I stand up quickly, my head spins and I feel faint. I also get out of breath easily just walking up a few steps, but no chest pain.
No, I have not noticed any easy bruising, pinpoint red spots on my legs, nosebleeds, or bleeding gums.
My appetite is a bit lower than usual because I feel so sluggish, but I have not had nausea or vomiting.
No, my weight has been completely steady at around sixty kilograms.
No, my fingers and toes do not turn pale or blue in the cold, and my symptoms did not start after being in a cold environment.
No joint swelling, facial rashes, hair loss, mouth sores, or known autoimmune disorders like lupus.
No, I have not eaten raw oysters, clams, or undercooked seafood recently, and nobody around me is jaundiced or sick.
I have never had hepatitis B or C, never had a blood transfusion, and I do not have any tattoos. I have never used intravenous drugs or shared needles, and I have a single long-term partner.
No, my belly has not swollen, and my shoes and ankles fit normally without any swelling.

My eyes turned yellow and my urine looks like tea, so I figured I must have caught hepatitis or bad food poisoning that attacked my liver. I'm scared to death that my liver is completely shutting down and I'll need a transplant, which would leave my kids without anyone to care for them.
I hope you can run some liver tests and give me something to clear this yellow color and get my energy back.
I have always been healthy. I have no history of anemia, liver problems, gallstones, or other chronic medical conditions.
I had an uncomplicated appendectomy when I was in college fifteen years ago. No other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I am not taking any prescription medications. I have not taken any antibiotics, pain pills, herbal decoctions, or dietary supplements recently.
No, I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two glasses of wine once or twice a month, and I have not had a drink in the past month.
I work full-time as an accountant in an office, and I live in an apartment with my husband.
No one in my family has had early jaundice, anemia, gallstones at a young age, or spleen enlargement.

My last menstrual period started two weeks ago and was normal. My cycles are regular every twenty-eight days, my husband had a vasectomy so there is no chance of pregnancy, and my flow has not been unusually heavy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and body temperature is 37.2 degrees Celsius.
Alert and oriented, but appears visibly pale, fatigued, and noticeably jaundiced.
Prominent scleral icterus bilaterally with marked conjunctival pallor; pupils equal, round, and reactive to light.
Pale oral mucous membranes; no oral ulcers, petechiae, or mucosal bleeding.
No palpable cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with an ejection systolic flow murmur at the left upper sternal border; no murmurs, gallops, or rubs.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular sounds and no rales, wheezing, or crackles.
Abdomen is soft, flat, and non-tender throughout; no guarding or rebound tenderness.
Murphy's sign is negative, with no localized right upper quadrant tenderness or palpable gallbladder.
The liver edge is not enlarged, but the spleen tip is palpably enlarged approximately two centimeters below the left costal margin on deep inspiration.
No shifting dullness or fluid wave; normal abdominal tympany throughout.
No asterixis or flapping tremor noted on bilateral hand extension.
Generalized jaundiced skin tone without spider angiomas, palmar erythema, excoriation scratch marks, petechiae, or purpura.
No pretibial or ankle pitting edema in either lower extremity.
